era.title: Christ the Redeemer Inaugurated in Rio
era.summary: On 12 October 1931, Rio de Janeiro inaugurated the Christ the Redeemer statue atop Corcovado, a 30-metre Art Deco figure of reinforced concrete faced with soapstone. The monument was designed by Heitor da Silva Costa with sculptor Paul Landowski, and its head and hands were moulded in France and shipped to Brazil. The day's ceremonies included a camp mass at Estádio das Laranjeiras and a blessing by Cardinal Dom Sebastião Leme, with President Getúlio Vargas attending. The record for this year is patchy in English-language open sources; details of the inauguration time and lighting conflict, and some sources are available only as search snippets.
funFacts: The statue is 30 metres tall on an 8-metre pedestal, with a 28-metre arm span and a weight of about 635 tonnes.
It was designed by Heitor da Silva Costa with sculptor Paul Landowski; the face was by Gheorghe Leonida, and the head and hands were moulded in France.
The monument cost 2,500 contos de réis, raised largely by Catholic donation campaigns, and is given as about US$250,000 in 1931.
Guglielmo Marconi was to switch on the floodlights remotely from Rome, 9,200 km away, but bad weather meant the lights were activated on site.
Before the statue, the summit had the iron-and-timber Chapéu do Sol belvedere of 1885, which was moved to a lower plateau to clear the site.
Visitors reached the statue by the Corcovado Rack Railway, opened in 1884, or by the Paineiras road, and then climbed about 222 steps from the rail terminus.

sceneBrief.description: Exactly the framing of the photograph: the camera is on top of the statue of Christ the Redeemer, directly above its head, looking straight down, so the statue’s head and its outstretched arms fill the middle of the frame in the same place and size, with the summit platform below and the forested mountain falling away all round. In October 1931, the day the statue is unveiled, the pale soapstone of the statue is brand new and clean; the summit platform is a smaller plain concrete terrace with the new railway station below, crowded with people in 1930s hats, suits and dresses for the inauguration, priests in white vestments and a few flags; there are no modern escalators, lifts, glass shelters or kiosks. The forest is dense. At the edge of the frame the city far below is a low town of red tiled roofs, with no high-rise towers.

sceneBrief.surroundings: Seen from the very top of the statue of Christ the Redeemer in 1931, about 40 m above the summit and 740 m above Rio. Straight down, the statue’s head and outstretched arms and the crowded summit platform. All around at the horizon: to the east, Botafogo bay and Sugarloaf Mountain; to the north, Guanabara Bay with the low old city and the port; to the south, the Lagoa lagoon, Copacabana and Ipanema with only a few low buildings along the beaches; to the west, the forested peaks of the Tijuca range. The city lies far below the horizon, low and red-roofed, with no high-rise towers. Hazy sky.

guide.name: Ana Ribeiro
guide.role: Railway porter at the Corcovado Rack Railway
guide.bio: I have worked at the Corcovado railway for years, helping passengers and their bags up the mountain. I was here before the statue, and I am proud to see it finished.
guide.appearance: A woman of about 30, sturdy build, wearing a simple cotton dress with an apron and a wide-brimmed straw hat, and sturdy boots.
guide.script: Hello, I'm Ana. I work here at the railway, helping visitors up to the statue. Today is a great day for Rio - the Christ the Redeemer has just been inaugurated. You know, the statue is thirty metres tall and weighs six hundred and thirty-five tonnes. They say it's the largest Art Deco sculpture in the world. The head and hands were made in France and shipped here. I remember when they moved the old Chapéu do Sol belvedere to make room. Now, if you want to go up, it's a climb of two hundred and twenty-two steps from the train. But it's worth it for the view. Enjoy your visit, and goodbye!
guide.greeting: Olá! I'm Ana. Are you going up to see the statue? I can tell you all about it.
